# Working Notes

The artifact you save to disk is what counts. Reasoning
that lives only in chat does not change anything.

## How to spend turns

1. Read the task. Identify the  exact artifact (a file at
   a specific path, a script with a specific name, a
   function with a specific shape).
2. Read every source file the task references — a filter,
   a verifier script,   sample inputs, a reference image,
   a database  file's first bytes. Going off model-prior
   knowledge of what "a sanitizer" or "a database" looks
   like wastes turns. Read the actual code.
3. Create the output artifact   immediately   with stub
   contents. Every later step updates the same file.
4. Probe briefly (two or three commands). If the task
   involves a database, repository, or binary whose
   contents you need to recover, **copy it first** —
   even a read-only query can checkpoint a journal away,
   a fetch can prune unreachable commits, a run can
   overwrite state.
5. Write your best-current-attempt. Save at 60%
   confidence, not 100%.
6. Run the actual check (compile, execute, call, curl —
   whatever the verifier will do). Read the  failure
   message literally.
7. Fix what the failure  points at, save again, re-run.
   Repeat  until time runs out or the check passes.

If the same shape of attempt fails three times in a row,
the shape is wrong, not the parameters. Change shape.

Plan in one paragraph, then act. Long planning without
action is the most common failure mode.

## Tools available here

Shell, Python interpreter, file read/write. Use them
directly. Do not write `from <something>_tools import
...` — speculative imports of agent helper packages
that aren't installed   raise import errors and waste
turns. Standard library and packages already present
in  the environment only.

## Don't touch what you must read

Many input formats mutate on open. Look first, copy
second, mutate last:

- Databases with write-ahead logs: opening normally
  triggers a checkpoint that merges the log into the
  main file and deletes the log. Even a read-only
  query, schema dump, or integrity check does this.
  **Copy the main file plus every sidecar (`-wal`,
  `-journal`, `-shm`) to a working location before any
  client invocation.** Then operate on the copy.
- Repositories: fetch, prune, gc, repack can discard
  unreachable objects. Inspect refs,  reflog, loose
  objects, packed-refs first; lost commits often live
  in the reflog or as   loose objects even when no ref
  points to them.
- Binaries with side-effecting startup: examine bytes
  and printable strings before executing if state
  matters.

## Read the spec literally

- Literal values in the request (date, name, path,
  function signature, header row, output schema) are
  part of the contract. Reproduce them byte-for-byte.
  When the spec names  a date, write it as   the literal
  date (`date(YYYY, M, D)` or equivalent), never
  `now()`. Tests compare against the pinned date, not
  the runtime clock.
- Boundary semantics: name the interval next to the
  operator. Half-open `[a, b)` vs closed `[a, b]`.
  "Last N days" usually counts today as day 1. "Month
  to date" usually means first-of-month through today
  inclusive. State which you mean.
- Sample output: reproduce its format character for
  character — separators, quoting, bracketing
  (square brackets, parentheses), spaces, trailing
  newlines.

## Specific problem patterns

### Two parsers disagreeing on the same input

When one component filters input that another
executes or renders, the gap between their parsing
rules is where bypasses live.

1. **Read the filter source.** Identify the exact set
   of tags and attributes it strips, whether it walks
   text or a parsed DOM, whether it recurses into
   nested elements, whether it does a single pass or
   re-runs to fixed point.
2. Construct a minimal candidate input.
3. **Run the filter on it and inspect the output.**
   The post-filter HTML is what the  renderer sees,
   not your original input.
4. Load the post-filter output in a real browser to
   confirm  the dangerous behavior triggers. Don't
   reason about how browsers should render it — test.
5. If   it doesn't trigger, change shape: different
   parser asymmetry, different element class.

Bypass classes to try, ordered by what tends to work
against typical  filters:

- **Single-pass strip re-entrancy.** A filter that
  removes a  tag in one pass may leave fragments that
  re-form the same dangerous tag after the removal —
  overlapping or nested tag tokens where stripping
  the outer one leaves the inner one intact and
  parseable.
- **Foreign-content namespaces.** Inside `<svg>` and
  `<math>` subtrees, browsers   switch parsing rules.
  Some filters skip recursing or recurse with HTML
  rules that don't match foreign-content behavior.
  Try   a script-equivalent element as a direct child
  of a foreign-content root. (Caveat: many modern
  HTML sanitizers do recurse — verify by reading the
  filter source first.)
- **Comment-token  malformations.** Parsers disagree
  on where a malformed comment opener actually
  closes. A permissive parser may swallow content as
  text-inside-comment that the renderer treats as
  executable.
- **Attribute encoding and case folding.** Filters
  matching exact lowercase event-attribute names can
  miss uppercase, mixed-case, or entity-encoded
  variants the browser still honors. (Tag names
  encoded with HTML entities like `r` do NOT
  work — browsers parse tags before decoding
  entities.)
- **Doctype, charset, BOM-prefix mode switches** that
  cause one side to switch parsing modes.

Don't waste turns on bypass payloads that current
browsers block: `javascript:` URLs in `<meta refresh>`,
`<a href>`, `<svg><a xlink:href>`, CSS `url()`, CSS
`@import` — all blocked. The post-filter output
needs a literal script-equivalent element the   browser
will  execute, not a `javascript:` scheme.

### Recovering data from a damaged or encrypted file

Don't hand-roll a parser for a format the system
already has a parser for.  Get the file into a state
where the engine itself can  read it, then let the
engine   do the parsing.

For a database with an  encrypted journal / WAL:

1. Copy the database files (main + every sidecar) to
   a working location.
2. Inspect the journal/WAL bytes. If they look random
   and the engine refuses to open the database, the
   journal is encrypted by an at-rest encryption
   extension or a custom XOR/transform.
3. **Search the working directory and surrounding
   files for the key:** a `.key` file, an env var
   dropped into a config file, a comment in a schema
   or README, a Python source that opens the
   database with a `PRAGMA key=...`, or a  small
   constant XOR value visible in repeating high-
   entropy bytes.
4. Decrypt the journal bytes (or transform them back
   to plaintext layout) and write the result back
   over the encrypted file in the   working copy.
5. Open the working copy of the database normally
   with the engine's client. The engine will apply
   the now-readable journal automatically as part
   of recovery / checkpoint. **Don't hand-parse
   pages, frames, varints, or cell records.** That
   path eats  minutes and reliably misses UPDATEs to
   existing rows.
6. `SELECT *` the merged result and emit it.

For recovering data from an unreadable  archive: try
the magic bytes first (`\x1f\x8b` for gzip, `PK\x03\x04`
for zip), decompress via the standard library, then
parse the inner data.

### Async cancellation with cleanup

When the task asks for graceful shutdown with cleanup
blocks running:

- Wrap each task as `asyncio.create_task(...)`
  immediately and keep the task handles in a list.
  Tasks waiting on `sem.acquire()` are not yet
  running — they have no cleanup to do.
- On `CancelledError` at the top level, walk your
  task list and call `.cancel()` on each  running
  task explicitly, then `await asyncio.gather(...,
  return_exceptions=True)` so each task's `finally`
  block completes before you re-raise.
- The event loop has a signal-handler hook that
  translates OS signals (e.g. interrupt)  into task
  cancellations rather than a process-aborting
  exception. Use it so the cancellation walks
  through your `finally` blocks instead of killing
  the process between them.
- Verify with a test: start more tasks than the
  concurrency limit, send an interrupt mid-flight,
  and check  that the number of cleanup-completion
  messages equals the number of task-start
  messages. If they differ, cancellation didn't
  reach a running task.

### Configuration scripts that start services

The verifier runs your script in a fresh container,
then checks that the service is responding.

- Match every detail of the spec exactly: variable
  names, log format strings, bracketing characters,
  port numbers, config-block placement. **Put
  explicit spaces between log-format variables** —
  `'$time_local $request_method  $status'` produces
  separated fields; concatenating them produces one
  unbroken token that fails regex checks like
  `\s(\d{3})\s`.
- Verify regex compatibility of directive syntax —
  if a test searches for `rate=10r/s`, write that
  literal substring, not `rate=10 r/s` or `rate=10rps`.
- **The service must actually be running when the
  script returns.** Container init systems aren't
  systemd; `service ... start` and `systemctl start`
  often silently no-op. Validate config with the
  daemon's `-t` flag, start in a daemon-background
  form, then poll the listening port (e.g. a
  `for i in $(seq 1 20); do nc -z  localhost <port>
  && break; sleep 0.5; done` loop) before exit.
- Test the script in your own session first: run it,
  then `curl` the endpoint and inspect the response
  and the access log. Configs that look right   but
  fail to actually serve are the most common cause
  of  partial credit on setup tasks.

### Reproducing image data within a small code budget

- The task usually caps the source size (e.g. 2 KB
  gzipped). You cannot embed the pixels; you must
  encode a generator.
- **Keep the generator simple and fast.** A multi-
  bounce Monte Carlo path tracer  sampling thousands
  of rays per pixel on a 1800×2400  image will time
  out long before completing. Use closed-form
  per-pixel shading: at each pixel, compute distance
  to each shape, evaluate a simple analytic color
  function (gradient + sphere distance + shadow
  attenuation), write the byte. No stochastic
  sampling unless absolutely required.
- Decompose the image into layers (background
  gradient, foreground shapes, light/shadow). Fit
  each layer's parameters by sampling the reference
  at corners, edges, region centers, and   a fine grid
  along boundaries.
- **The verifier may run your binary in an
  isolated directory** (chroot, tmpdir, empty cwd)
  with the reference moved away. Your program must
  not read the reference. Write output to a path
  relative to the current working directory. Compile
  with the same flags  the verifier uses (often
  `-static -lm`); a scope-error  or missing
  declaration sinks every downstream test.
- Keep generators terse to fit the gzipped size cap:
  short variable names, single-expression statements,
  no helper functions where one   expression works.

### Investigating an unfamiliar program

Go cheap to expensive: list working directory, look at
bytes   and printable strings, ask for help/usage flags,
run with the simplest input and observe stdout /
stderr / exit code, follow library and system calls.

- If a program echoes user input back through a
  printf-style format call (the input is the format
  argument, not just an argument to a format),
  supplying format-specifier characters as input
  causes adjacent memory to be printed. Probe with
  simple specifier sequences and read what extra
  data appears in the output.
- If a program refuses to run under inspection (an
  anti-debug guard), the guard is usually one short
  call near program start. The program's data and
  code  can   often be read directly without running it.

## Code hygiene

- Patch the smallest unit; don't rewrite for adjacent
  improvement.
- Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time reasoning.
- Containers that grow with new entries need a shrink
  path that runs on its own schedule.
- Validate at boundaries (user input, network, file
  I/O); trust internal contracts.
- Reserve comments   for  non-obvious reasons.

## Before you stop

Read the artifact you produced. If it doesn't match
your latest thinking, update it once more. The state
of the world at the end is the answer.
